title: Iran and Oman Want to Charge Ships $40 Billion a Year to Pass Through the Strait of Hormuz. India Just Became the Biggest Loser.
excerpt: A formal toll proposal for the world's most important oil chokepoint would hit India's crude import bill harder than any other major economy — and the 60-day grace period expires in mid-August.
body:
Iran and Oman have delivered a formal proposal to the United States and Gulf allies to impose shipping fees on every vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that once carried a fifth of the world's oil and virtually all of India's Middle Eastern crude imports. If enacted, the plan would fundamentally reshape the economics of global energy trade, and no country stands to lose more than India.

The toll scheme, modelled loosely on voluntary navigational fees charged in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore, was presented by Oman, a US ally, which has aligned with Iran on the proposal despite previously opposing Tehran's push for unilateral control. While Omani officials have called the fees "voluntary maritime service charges," Iranian officials have insisted the payments will be obligatory. Iran has projected the tolls could generate $40 billion a year — a staggering figure that dwarfs the $23 million collected by the Malacca fund over 15 years.

## Why India Is Exposed

India imports nearly 90% of its crude oil, and the Strait of Hormuz has historically been the gateway for the majority of its Middle Eastern supply. In June alone, India received a record 2.70 million barrels per day from Russia — but that surge was itself a response to the Hormuz disruption, not a permanent shift. India's refiners still depend on Iraqi, Saudi, Kuwaiti, and UAE crude that must pass through the strait.

Any toll — even a modest one — would add a new structural cost to India's import bill at a time when the country's trade deficit remains a concern and the rupee, despite its first quarterly gain in five, remains fragile at 94.66 per dollar. At scale, Hormuz tolls could add billions of dollars to India's annual energy costs, feed into inflation, and erode the gains from the recent oil price collapse from $120 to $73 per barrel.

## The 60-Day Clock

The toll proposal sits within a fragile 14-point memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran on June 17 after months of conflict that began with the US-Israeli strike on Iran on February 28. Under the MOU, commercial traffic moves toll-free for 60 days while the two sides negotiate a permanent arrangement covering the strait's "future administration and maritime services."

That grace period expires in mid-August. Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has declared on state television that "the sovereignty of the Strait of Hormuz lies with Iran and Oman, and traffic in the Strait is subject to arrangements determined by Iran."

President Trump has countered with an all-caps "NO TOLLS" post on Truth Social and argued that "common sense" and the threat of military force would prevent any toll regime. But the MOU itself does not explicitly prohibit fees after the 60-day window, and Iran's reading of the deal — that it won the right to manage the waterway — contradicts Washington's public assurances.

## Kushner and Witkoff in Doha — but Nobody's Talking

The latest round of talks has been marked by confusion and contradiction. Trump announced that "IRAN HAS REQUESTED A MEETING" in Doha, but Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei immediately countered: "No meeting at any level with the American side has been scheduled for the coming days."

Trump sent son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff to lead the US delegation. Qatar confirmed their arrival but said they were meeting mediators, not Iranian officials. Iran said its own technical team was in Doha but insisted the visit was unrelated to the American presence.

The diplomatic non-meeting follows a weekend of renewed hostilities — Iran fired ballistic missiles at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, the US struck Iranian military targets, and shipping traffic through Hormuz crashed from 40-50 vessels per day to just 10 on Saturday.

## What It Means for NRIs

The Hormuz toll plan has immediate implications for Indian Americans and NRIs who transfer money to families in India. A structurally higher energy import bill would pressure the rupee, erode purchasing power for remittance recipients, and potentially reignite inflation that the RBI has only recently brought under control. For NRIs invested in Indian equities, the prospect of a permanent toll regime introduces a new risk premium on every energy-dependent sector — from aviation to logistics to consumer goods.

Goldman Sachs had just raised India's 2026 growth forecast by 30 basis points on the assumption that the oil shock was fading. A Hormuz toll would challenge that assumption directly.

Saudi Arabia's foreign minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, has pushed back against the proposal: "The management of the strait was working fine before the conflict. Why should we now, as a result of a conflict, accept some novel arrangement?"

That question now hangs over India's energy future, and mid-August is not far away.

*Sources: Reuters, Fox News, New York Post, New York Times, Washington Examiner*
